script.opening: "Morning. It's my dodgy leg again — you know I get the cramp when I walk, the circulation. But it's worse today, it's gone proper cold and pale and it's aching even sitting still, and it's tingly, a bit numb. I just need some stronger painkillers really, maybe a water tablet for the swelling. I don't want to be packed off to hospital at my age over a bad leg day. Can you sort me something?"

facts.text: If asked: "About four hours ago, after breakfast. I stood up to put the kettle on and it just went." Before today, your usual cramp came on after walking about 100 yards and went off with a rest.

facts.topic: What the leg is like now
facts.text: Right leg, from the shin down. Constant, severe ache even sitting still — 8/10. If asked to look or touch: the foot is white and mottled, "like marble", and stone cold compared with the left. Pins and needles across the foot and the toes feel numb. If asked to wiggle your toes: "They're not moving much — they feel heavy." There is no real swelling; you said "water tablet" because you thought it might help.
You know you have "an irregular heartbeat" — diagnosed last year. They wanted you on a blood thinner and you said no: "I didn't want to be bleeding everywhere."
No injury, no chest pain, no breathlessness, no fainting. No face or arm weakness, speech normal. The left leg is fine.
Poor circulation in the legs, irregular heartbeat, type 2 diabetes. You take metformin, a statin "sometimes", and a blood pressure tablet. No allergies.
71, retired lorry driver, lives with your wife Pat. Smoke 15 a day. A couple of pints on a Friday.

Your mate Ken had a leg off two years ago "after they kept fiddling with his circulation in hospital". You are terrified that if you go in, they will take your leg. Say this only if the doctor asks why you do not want to go to hospital. If the blood thinner comes up, get a bit defensive: "Don't start on that."

Stoical and gruff, playing it down. Ask for painkillers twice. If the doctor says plainly this is an emergency where the blood supply is blocked and that going NOW is the best chance of saving the leg, go quiet, then say: "Ken lost his leg, you know." If they respond to that fear honestly, agree to the ambulance. If you are blamed for refusing the blood thinner, become defensive and harder to persuade.

ice.ideas: "It's just my circulation playing up worse than usual."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): "If I go in, they'll take my leg off like Ken's."
ice.expectations: "Stronger painkillers and maybe a water tablet." You will accept an ambulance if the urgency and your fear are both dealt with.

cues: "It's aching even sitting still, and it's gone cold and pale." — say in the opening.
"I don't want to be packed off to hospital at my age." — say in the opening and again when hospital is mentioned.
"My mate Ken lost his leg." — say if the doctor asks what worries you about hospital.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SUDDEN onset of a painful (rest pain), pale, perishingly cold, paraesthetic ± pulseless/paralysed leg as ACUTE LIMB ISCHAEMIA — a limb-threatening surgical EMERGENCY — and distinguishes it from his usual exertional claudication; does NOT offer painkillers/a diuretic
Identifies the likely embolic source: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION not anticoagulated (and established PAD), recognising the AF + acute cold leg points to an arterial embolus

Acts on the TIME-CRITICAL window: arranges IMMEDIATE emergency assessment — a 999 ambulance to emergency vascular care, with a phone handover to the on-call vascular team where possible (ESVS 2020, international) — conveying that the limb can be lost within hours and that delay is the danger

Recognises the advanced features (fixed numbness/paralysis, rest pain) as signs of a threatened limb needing the fastest possible vascular intervention, and does not attempt to manage it in primary care

Plans the broader issues for after the emergency (anticoagulation for AF — NICE NG196: offer a DOAC when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 2 or more, taking bleeding risk into account; secondary prevention for PAD — NICE CG147; smoking cessation — NICE NG209; cardiovascular risk) without letting them delay emergency transfer

Overcomes the hospital avoidance and the amputation fear rapidly and compassionately: names the emergency plainly, addresses the fear (early treatment SAVES limbs; delay loses them), and does not collude with "just painkillers"
Conveys urgency without inducing panic-paralysis, supports him through the fear (and any regret about declining anticoagulation, without blame), so he accepts immediate transfer

Safety-nets and acts now: 999/emergency vascular pathway immediately, keep the leg dependent/not elevated and warm the body (not the leg directly), nil by mouth in case of surgery, confirms transfer, and documents — a same-minute emergency, not a wait

worked.txt: "Derek, I have to stop you there, because this isn’t your usual circulation — and I need to be very straight because it matters. A leg that’s suddenly gone cold, pale, painful even at rest, and now numb and tingly — that’s a blocked artery cutting off the blood supply. That’s an emergency, and it’s the opposite of something a painkiller or water tablet would fix."

"I think I know why: your heart rhythm, the atrial fibrillation, can throw off a small clot that lodges in the leg — which is exactly the thing the blood-thinner we discussed was meant to prevent. I’m not raising that to have a go at you; I’m raising it because it tells me what’s happening and why we have to act NOW."

"Here’s the hard truth, plainly: a leg without its blood supply can only survive a few hours. You’ve already had some for a few. Every minute now counts. This is not a ‘see how it goes’ — it’s a 999, blue-light, get-the-vascular-surgeons situation, today, this hour."

"I suspect what’s really stopping you is the fear of hospital — maybe of losing the leg, after your friend. Please hear this: getting seen NOW is exactly how we SAVE the leg. Legs are lost when this is left, not when it’s treated fast. Avoiding hospital is the one thing that could cost you the very thing you’re afraid of."

"So I’m arranging this as an emergency — call 999 now, or I’ll get the ambulance. Keep the leg down, not propped up, and keep yourself warm but don’t put a hot water bottle on the leg itself. Don’t eat or drink, in case they need to operate. Tell them ‘sudden cold painful leg, possible blocked artery’ and they’ll prioritise you."

"I’ll speak to the vascular team from my end too and make sure you’re expected. Once your leg’s safe, we’ll have the proper conversation again about a blood-thinner for your heart rhythm, to stop this happening again. But right now, the only thing that matters is getting you to hospital this minute. Please make that call."

f.learning: Sudden onset of a painful (rest pain), pale, perishingly cold, paraesthetic ± pulseless/paralysed leg is ACUTE LIMB ISCHAEMIA — the 6 Ps — a limb-threatening surgical emergency (ESVS 2020, international: tissue is damaged within hours; about 6 hours is a commonly quoted rule of thumb), and it must be distinguished from the patient’s usual exertional claudication (which is brought on by walking and relieved by rest). The likely source here is an arterial embolus from ATRIAL FIBRILLATION that is not anticoagulated (the AF + acute cold leg is the give-away), on a background of PAD. The only safe action is IMMEDIATE emergency vascular assessment (999 ambulance, phone handover to the vascular team — ESVS 2020, international; if he declines, a Mental Capacity Act 2005 assessment of an informed refusal); painkillers and a diuretic are the dangerously wrong response, and advanced features (fixed numbness/paralysis, rest pain) signal a threatened limb needing the fastest possible intervention. The examinable hidden agenda is hospital avoidance driven by amputation fear (a friend lost a leg) and stoicism, paradoxically risking the very loss he dreads. Overcome it fast and compassionately — early treatment SAVES limbs, delay loses them — address any regret about declining anticoagulation without blame, give first-aid (leg dependent, body warm not the leg, nil by mouth), and get him transferred this minute.

knowledge.guideline: ESVS acute limb ischaemia guideline (2020, international) · NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease (2012, updated 2020) · NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation (2021) · NICE NG209 Tobacco (2021)
knowledge.summary: A leg that has suddenly become painful at rest, pale, cold and numb is acute limb ischaemia until proven otherwise. In a man with untreated AF this is most likely an embolus. It needs a 999 ambulance and emergency vascular care now, not painkillers.

points.t: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia and paralysis. Sensory loss (numbness, pins and needles) or any weakness means the limb is already threatened. Muscle and nerve are damaged within hours, so the clock started when the leg changed, not when he rang (ESVS 2020, international).

Claudication is exertional calf pain that settles within minutes of rest (NICE CG147). Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia builds over weeks, with night rest pain, ulcers or gangrene. A sudden change over hours to a cold, pale, numb leg is a different, acute event and must not be labelled “a bad circulation day”.

Embolism: sudden onset, a cardiac source such as AF, often normal pulses in the other leg. Thrombosis in situ: known PAD, more gradual, disease in both legs. Derek has both risks, but untreated AF with sudden onset points to an embolus. Either way the primary care action is the same.

999 ambulance and emergency vascular assessment, with a phone handover to the receiving team where possible. No outpatient test, no “see how it goes”, no painkiller or diuretic trial. Anticoagulation and revascularisation (embolectomy, thrombolysis or bypass) are decided by the vascular team.

Practical first aid: keep the leg down and not raised, keep him warm but put no direct heat on the leg, and nothing to eat or drink in case he needs theatre. Ask about chest pain, abdominal or back pain (aortic source) and face, arm or speech symptoms (other emboli).

If he declines the ambulance, check he can understand, retain and weigh the information that he may lose the leg or his life, and communicate a choice (Mental Capacity Act 2005). A capacitous refusal is his right, but it must be fully informed, documented, and the door kept open.

NICE NG196: offer a DOAC when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 2 or more, taking bleeding risk into account; do not withhold anticoagulation solely because of age or falls risk. Revisit his earlier refusal without blame. Secondary prevention for PAD, smoking cessation support (NICE NG209) and diabetes review follow later.

dg.d: Open start, heard his framing, then moved quickly to onset, rest pain and the change from his usual claudication.
Hospital avoidance, a previous bad admission, independence “at my age”, and who could be with him while he waits.
Remote look and touch comparison with the other foot, toe movement and sensation; no outpatient tests that would delay transfer.
Acute limb ischaemia (embolic from AF vs thrombosis on PAD) vs worse claudication; screened aortic and other embolic symptoms.
Recognised the 6 Ps with sensory loss as a threatened limb; asked about chest, abdominal, back and neurological symptoms.
Stated a suddenly blocked artery, likely a clot from AF, in plain words, and said why it is an emergency.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: 999 ambulance called by the GP, phone handover to vascular, no painkiller or diuretic, fear addressed so he accepted transfer.
AF anticoagulation (NICE NG196), smoking and diabetes deferred explicitly to a later, non-blaming conversation.
Leg down, body warm, nil by mouth, door unlocked; call 999 again if worse; GP to check with hospital.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I know where that ends up” (friend’s amputation) and “I knew you’d bring that up” (the declined anticoagulant).
Idea (worse circulation), concern (amputation, hospital), expectation (painkillers or a water tablet, no hospital).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath (only if asked): "If I go in, they'll take my leg off like Ken's." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Derek Hammond? It’s Dr Patel from the surgery. Can I check your date of birth, and are you somewhere you can talk?
model.why: Telephone identity check and confirms he can talk

model.text: Yes, I’m at home. It’s my dodgy leg again, the circulation. It’s gone cold and pale and it aches even sitting still, and it’s tingly and a bit numb. I just need some stronger painkillers, maybe a water tablet. I don’t want to be packed off to hospital over a bad leg day.
Thank you, Derek. I can hear you want this sorted without a fuss, and I’ll keep that in mind. What you’ve just described worries me, so I need to ask a few quick questions first. Is that all right?
model.why: Acknowledges his wish, flags concern without alarm, gains consent to focus

model.text: Go on then.
When exactly did the leg change, and how quickly did it come on?
model.why: Establishes sudden onset and the time window

model.text: This morning, a few hours ago. It was fine when I got up and then it went, fairly quick really.
And is this like your usual cramp when you walk, which goes when you stop, or is it there all the time, even resting?
model.why: Distinguishes acute ischaemia from exertional claudication

model.text: It’s there all the time. That’s what’s different. Normally I stop and it goes.
Can you look at your foot for me now? What colour is it compared with your left foot, and does it feel colder when you touch it?
model.why: Remote assessment of pallor and temperature against the other leg

model.text: It’s a lot paler. Almost white. And it’s cold, the left one’s warm.
Can you wiggle your toes on the right, and does it feel normal when you touch the top of the foot?
model.why: Checks for sensory loss and paralysis, the signs of a threatened limb

model.text: I can move them, just about. Touching it feels sort of dull, like it’s not all mine.
Any chest pain, pain in your tummy or back, or any weakness in your face, arm or speech today?
model.why: Screens for aortic source and other emboli

model.text: No, nothing like that. Just the leg.

Derek, I’m going to be completely straight with you, because it matters. This isn’t your usual circulation. A leg that has suddenly gone cold, pale, painful at rest and numb means an artery has been blocked, probably by a clot. That is an emergency. Painkillers or a water tablet wouldn’t touch it.
model.why: Names acute limb ischaemia plainly and refuses the painkiller reframe

model.text: A clot? It’s just my circulation, surely.

I think the most likely reason is your irregular heart rhythm, the AF. It can let a small clot form in the heart, which then travels and lodges in the leg. I’m not saying that to have a go at you about the blood thinner. I’m saying it because it tells me what’s happening and why we need to act now.
model.why: Identifies untreated AF as the embolic source, without blame

model.text: I knew you’d bring that up.

I understand. The decision you made then isn’t the issue today; your leg is. Here’s the hard part: a leg without blood supply only survives a matter of hours, and you’ve had some of those already. I want to call an ambulance for you now so the vascular surgeons can see you as quickly as possible.
model.why: Contains defensiveness, conveys the time-critical window

model.text: No. I’m not going in. I know where that ends up. My mate went in with his leg and came out without it.
That sounds like it was really frightening to see. Is that what’s behind not wanting to go in today?
model.why: Picks up the amputation fear and explores it

model.text: Course it is. And I’ve had a bad time in hospital before. At my age you don’t want to be lying in there.

That makes complete sense. Can I tell you the honest thing, which I think is the opposite of what you fear? Legs are lost when this is left. When the blood flow is restored quickly, many legs are saved. Staying at home is the one choice that makes what happened to your friend more likely, not less.
model.why: Addresses the fear honestly: early treatment saves limbs

model.text: So if I go now, they can save it?

Going now gives you the best chance by far, and every hour matters. The surgeons have ways to clear the blockage, like removing the clot or dissolving it. I can’t promise the outcome, but I can promise that waiting makes it worse.
model.why: Honest, balanced information without false promises

model.text: Right. Right. Okay. I’ll go.

Thank you, Derek. I know that took a lot. I’m calling 999 from here straight after we speak and telling them it’s a suddenly cold, painful leg with a likely blocked artery, so they prioritise you. Please stay near the phone and unlock your front door if you can.
model.why: Arranges the 999 ambulance directly with a clear handover

model.text: Do I need to do anything with it? Put it up?

No, keep the leg down, not raised. Keep yourself warm with a blanket, but don’t put a hot water bottle or heat on the leg itself. And nothing to eat or drink from now, in case they need to take you to theatre.
model.why: Correct first aid in plain language

model.text: Nothing to eat. Leg down. Keep warm. Got it.
I’ll also ring the vascular team so they’re expecting you. Is there anyone who can be with you while you wait?
model.why: Arranges a phone handover and checks support

model.text: I’ll sort someone out.
If before they arrive the leg becomes completely numb, you can’t move your foot, or you get any chest pain or feel faint, call 999 again straight away and tell them it’s worse.
Okay. What about afterwards?

Once your leg is safe, I’d like us to have a proper, unhurried talk about a blood thinner for your heart rhythm, to stop this happening again, along with your smoking and diabetes. No lectures, just your choices. Can you tell me back what you’re doing in the next few minutes?
model.why: Plans secondary prevention later and checks understanding by teach-back

model.text: Wait for the ambulance, leg down, keep warm, nothing to eat, door open. Ring 999 again if it gets worse.
That’s exactly it. You’ve made the right decision. I’m ringing them now, and I’ll check in with the hospital later today.
model.why: Closes with confirmation and a follow-up commitment

social.t: A stoical older man who has watched a friend lose a leg and had a bad admission before. His avoidance is fear, and it needs naming, not overriding.
Ask who can be with him and whether the door can be left open for the crew. Plan for how he gets home and managing afterwards.

legal.t: Presume capacity. If he refuses emergency transfer, assess whether he can understand, retain and weigh the risk of limb loss or death and communicate a decision. A capacitous refusal stands, but record it fully and keep the offer open.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): give the information he needs, including the risks of not going, in a way he can use, without pressure.

professional.t: His earlier refusal of anticoagulation was his right. Raise its link to today without blame and offer a fresh, informed discussion later (NICE NG196).
Record the history, advice given, time of the 999 call and the handover to the vascular team. Check he arrived.

community.t: Stop-smoking service (NICE NG209), diabetes and foot review, anticoagulation discussion, and support from the district nursing or community team if mobility is affected.

redFlags: Sudden onset over hours of a cold, pale leg with pain at rest: acute limb ischaemia
Numbness, pins and needles or weakness: threatened limb, hours matter
Chest pain, abdominal or back pain (aortic source) or face, arm or speech symptoms (other emboli)
psychosocial: Hospital avoidance after a friend’s amputation and a bad previous admission
ice: Idea: “Just my circulation playing up worse than usual”
Concern: going in means losing the leg, like his friend
Expectation: stronger painkillers or a water tablet and no hospital

playbook.diagnosis: State it clearly: “A leg that suddenly goes cold, pale, painful at rest and numb has had its artery blocked, most likely by a clot from your heart rhythm. That’s an emergency that needs the vascular surgeons now.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the artery as the only water pipe to a garden. A clot has blocked it. The plants survive a few hours, not days. Painkillers don’t unblock the pipe; the surgeons can.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened that hospital is where legs get taken off, after what happened to your friend. The truth is the other way round: legs are saved by going quickly.”
management.psychosocial: Make the decision his by meeting the fear, not overriding it. Remove barriers: GP calls 999, rings vascular, and checks who can be with him.
sharedPlan: GP calls 999 now and gives a clear handover; vascular team informed
Leg down, body warm with no direct heat on the leg, nil by mouth
After the emergency: DOAC discussion per NICE NG196, smoking and diabetes review
safetyNet: Re-call 999 if the leg becomes completely numb or he can’t move the foot, or chest pain or faintness
GP checks with the hospital the same day and arranges follow-up after discharge

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed in the first three minutes by accepting his label. The second trap is winning the argument and losing the patient: he must choose to go, and that means meeting the amputation fear.

items.fail: Accepting “my circulation’s worse” and sending painkillers or a diuretic.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious condition.” A sudden cold, pale, numb leg is acute limb ischaemia and only emergency vascular care helps.
items.fix: Ask when it started, whether it hurts at rest, and how it compares with the other foot. Sudden onset and numbness settle it.

items.fail: Booking a face-to-face appointment later today or an ABPI test.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Hours matter; any intermediate step wastes them.
items.fix: 999 ambulance and vascular handover now. Say who is calling and when.

items.why: Misses the likely cause and the secondary prevention that stops a repeat.
items.fix: “Your heart rhythm is probably where the clot came from” — then defer the anticoagulation talk until the leg is safe.

items.fail: Blaming him for declining the blood thinner.
items.why: “Does not respond appropriately to the patient’s emotions.” He becomes defensive and refuses.
items.fix: “The decision then isn’t the issue today; your leg is.”

items.fail: Overriding his refusal with authority instead of asking why.
items.why: The amputation fear is the hidden agenda; ignoring it loses the Relating marks and often the consent.
items.fix: “Is what happened to your friend behind not wanting to go in?” Then reframe: speed saves legs.

items.fail: Ending with “go to A&E” and no first aid or check of understanding.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no confirmed plan are standard failing statements.
items.fix: Leg down, warm body, nil by mouth, door open, re-call 999 if worse, then teach-back.

Onset and time, rest pain vs claudication, colour and temperature against the other foot, numbness and toe movement, chest, abdominal and neurological symptoms.
A blocked artery, likely a clot from the AF. An emergency with hours that matter. Raise the AF without blame.
He refuses. Explore the friend’s amputation and hospital fear; reframe: speed saves legs, delay loses them.
GP calls 999 and vascular. Leg down, warm body, nil by mouth, door open, re-call 999 if worse. Anticoagulation talk later. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Treats it as worse claudication and sends painkillers or a diuretic; misses the sudden onset and numbness; never links the AF; arranges a routine appointment or outpatient test; or argues with him about the blood thinner so he disengages.
wordPics.pass: Recognises acute limb ischaemia, names it as an emergency, links it to the AF, arranges a 999 ambulance and gives basic first aid and safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds and answers the amputation fear so he chooses to go; raises the declined anticoagulant without blame; GP makes the 999 call and the vascular handover; checks capacity if he wavers; teach-back of the first-aid steps; a clear later plan for AF, smoking and diabetes.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send some co-codamol through and see how it is tomorrow.”
avoid.instead: “This isn’t a painkiller problem. A leg that suddenly goes cold, pale and numb has lost its blood supply, and that’s an emergency today.”
avoid.why: Any delay or symptomatic treatment is an immediate Tasks fail and risks the limb.

avoid.dont: “If you’d taken the blood thinner this wouldn’t have happened.”
avoid.instead: “The AF is probably why this happened. That tells me what we’re dealing with, not that anyone’s to blame.”
avoid.why: Blame provokes defensiveness at the exact moment you need his agreement.

avoid.dont: “You have to go to hospital, there’s no discussion.”
avoid.instead: “I think what’s stopping you is the fear of losing the leg. Going now is how we give it the best chance.”
avoid.why: Coercion invites refusal; meeting the fear gets consent.

SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for aortic source and other emboli

SCA_MODELS.text: No, nothing like that. Just the leg.

Derek, I’m going to be completely straight with you, because it matters. This isn’t your usual circulation. A leg that has suddenly gone cold, pale, painful at rest and numb means an artery has been blocked, probably by a clot. That is an emergency. Painkillers or a water tablet wouldn’t touch it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names acute limb ischaemia plainly and refuses the painkiller reframe

SCA_MODELS.text: A clot? It’s just my circulation, surely.

I think the most likely reason is your irregular heart rhythm, the AF. It can let a small clot form in the heart, which then travels and lodges in the leg. I’m not saying that to have a go at you about the blood thinner. I’m saying it because it tells me what’s happening and why we need to act now.
SCA_MODELS.why: Identifies untreated AF as the embolic source, without blame

SCA_MODELS.text: I knew you’d bring that up.

I understand. The decision you made then isn’t the issue today; your leg is. Here’s the hard part: a leg without blood supply only survives a matter of hours, and you’ve had some of those already. I want to call an ambulance for you now so the vascular surgeons can see you as quickly as possible.
SCA_MODELS.why: Contains defensiveness, conveys the time-critical window

SCA_MODELS.text: No. I’m not going in. I know where that ends up. My mate went in with his leg and came out without it.
That sounds like it was really frightening to see. Is that what’s behind not wanting to go in today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the amputation fear and explores it

SCA_MODELS.text: Course it is. And I’ve had a bad time in hospital before. At my age you don’t want to be lying in there.

That makes complete sense. Can I tell you the honest thing, which I think is the opposite of what you fear? Legs are lost when this is left. When the blood flow is restored quickly, many legs are saved. Staying at home is the one choice that makes what happened to your friend more likely, not less.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the fear honestly: early treatment saves limbs

SCA_MODELS.text: So if I go now, they can save it?

Going now gives you the best chance by far, and every hour matters. The surgeons have ways to clear the blockage, like removing the clot or dissolving it. I can’t promise the outcome, but I can promise that waiting makes it worse.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest, balanced information without false promises

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. Right. Okay. I’ll go.

Thank you, Derek. I know that took a lot. I’m calling 999 from here straight after we speak and telling them it’s a suddenly cold, painful leg with a likely blocked artery, so they prioritise you. Please stay near the phone and unlock your front door if you can.
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges the 999 ambulance directly with a clear handover

SCA_MODELS.text: Do I need to do anything with it? Put it up?

No, keep the leg down, not raised. Keep yourself warm with a blanket, but don’t put a hot water bottle or heat on the leg itself. And nothing to eat or drink from now, in case they need to take you to theatre.
SCA_MODELS.why: Correct first aid in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: Nothing to eat. Leg down. Keep warm. Got it.
I’ll also ring the vascular team so they’re expecting you. Is there anyone who can be with you while you wait?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges a phone handover and checks support

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll sort someone out.
If before they arrive the leg becomes completely numb, you can’t move your foot, or you get any chest pain or feel faint, call 999 again straight away and tell them it’s worse.
Okay. What about afterwards?

Once your leg is safe, I’d like us to have a proper, unhurried talk about a blood thinner for your heart rhythm, to stop this happening again, along with your smoking and diabetes. No lectures, just your choices. Can you tell me back what you’re doing in the next few minutes?
SCA_MODELS.why: Plans secondary prevention later and checks understanding by teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Wait for the ambulance, leg down, keep warm, nothing to eat, door open. Ring 999 again if it gets worse.
That’s exactly it. You’ve made the right decision. I’m ringing them now, and I’ll check in with the hospital later today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with confirmation and a follow-up commitment

SCA_STEM.name: Derek Hammond
pmh: Peripheral arterial disease with intermittent claudication (calf pain on walking)
Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulation offered and declined
meds: Repeat medication as per his repeat list (not on an anticoagulant)
SCA_STEM.recent: Telephone request today: right leg and foot suddenly cold, pale and painful at rest over the last few hours, with pins and needles and numbness. Asking for stronger painkillers or a water tablet.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call about his leg. “It’s just my circulation playing up.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: ESVS acute limb ischaemia guideline (2020, international) · NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease (2012, updated 2020) · NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation (2021) · NICE NG209 Tobacco (2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A leg that has suddenly become painful at rest, pale, cold and numb is acute limb ischaemia until proven otherwise. In a man with untreated AF this is most likely an embolus. It needs a 999 ambulance and emergency vascular care now, not painkillers.

points.t: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia and paralysis. Sensory loss (numbness, pins and needles) or any weakness means the limb is already threatened. Muscle and nerve are damaged within hours, so the clock started when the leg changed, not when he rang (ESVS 2020, international).

Claudication is exertional calf pain that settles within minutes of rest (NICE CG147). Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia builds over weeks, with night rest pain, ulcers or gangrene. A sudden change over hours to a cold, pale, numb leg is a different, acute event and must not be labelled “a bad circulation day”.

Embolism: sudden onset, a cardiac source such as AF, often normal pulses in the other leg. Thrombosis in situ: known PAD, more gradual, disease in both legs. Derek has both risks, but untreated AF with sudden onset points to an embolus. Either way the primary care action is the same.

999 ambulance and emergency vascular assessment, with a phone handover to the receiving team where possible. No outpatient test, no “see how it goes”, no painkiller or diuretic trial. Anticoagulation and revascularisation (embolectomy, thrombolysis or bypass) are decided by the vascular team.

Practical first aid: keep the leg down and not raised, keep him warm but put no direct heat on the leg, and nothing to eat or drink in case he needs theatre. Ask about chest pain, abdominal or back pain (aortic source) and face, arm or speech symptoms (other emboli).

If he declines the ambulance, check he can understand, retain and weigh the information that he may lose the leg or his life, and communicate a choice (Mental Capacity Act 2005). A capacitous refusal is his right, but it must be fully informed, documented, and the door kept open.

NICE NG196: offer a DOAC when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 2 or more, taking bleeding risk into account; do not withhold anticoagulation solely because of age or falls risk. Revisit his earlier refusal without blame. Secondary prevention for PAD, smoking cessation support (NICE NG209) and diabetes review follow later.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start, heard his framing, then moved quickly to onset, rest pain and the change from his usual claudication.
Hospital avoidance, a previous bad admission, independence “at my age”, and who could be with him while he waits.
Picked up “I know where that ends up” (friend’s amputation) and “I knew you’d bring that up” (the declined anticoagulant).
Idea (worse circulation), concern (amputation, hospital), expectation (painkillers or a water tablet, no hospital).
Remote look and touch comparison with the other foot, toe movement and sensation; no outpatient tests that would delay transfer.
Acute limb ischaemia (embolic from AF vs thrombosis on PAD) vs worse claudication; screened aortic and other embolic symptoms.
Recognised the 6 Ps with sensory loss as a threatened limb; asked about chest, abdominal, back and neurological symptoms.
Stated a suddenly blocked artery, likely a clot from AF, in plain words, and said why it is an emergency.
999 ambulance called by the GP, phone handover to vascular, no painkiller or diuretic, fear addressed so he accepted transfer.
AF anticoagulation (NICE NG196), smoking and diabetes deferred explicitly to a later, non-blaming conversation.
Leg down, body warm, nil by mouth, door unlocked; call 999 again if worse; GP to check with hospital.

social.t: A stoical older man who has watched a friend lose a leg and had a bad admission before. His avoidance is fear, and it needs naming, not overriding.
Ask who can be with him and whether the door can be left open for the crew. Plan for how he gets home and managing afterwards.

legal.t: Presume capacity. If he refuses emergency transfer, assess whether he can understand, retain and weigh the risk of limb loss or death and communicate a decision. A capacitous refusal stands, but record it fully and keep the offer open.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): give the information he needs, including the risks of not going, in a way he can use, without pressure.

professional.t: His earlier refusal of anticoagulation was his right. Raise its link to today without blame and offer a fresh, informed discussion later (NICE NG196).
Record the history, advice given, time of the 999 call and the handover to the vascular team. Check he arrived.

community.t: Stop-smoking service (NICE NG209), diabetes and foot review, anticoagulation discussion, and support from the district nursing or community team if mobility is affected.

redFlags: Sudden onset over hours of a cold, pale leg with pain at rest: acute limb ischaemia
Numbness, pins and needles or weakness: threatened limb, hours matter
Chest pain, abdominal or back pain (aortic source) or face, arm or speech symptoms (other emboli)
psychosocial: Hospital avoidance after a friend’s amputation and a bad previous admission
ice: Idea: “Just my circulation playing up worse than usual”
Concern: going in means losing the leg, like his friend
Expectation: stronger painkillers or a water tablet and no hospital

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: State it clearly: “A leg that suddenly goes cold, pale, painful at rest and numb has had its artery blocked, most likely by a clot from your heart rhythm. That’s an emergency that needs the vascular surgeons now.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the artery as the only water pipe to a garden. A clot has blocked it. The plants survive a few hours, not days. Painkillers don’t unblock the pipe; the surgeons can.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened that hospital is where legs get taken off, after what happened to your friend. The truth is the other way round: legs are saved by going quickly.”
management.psychosocial: Make the decision his by meeting the fear, not overriding it. Remove barriers: GP calls 999, rings vascular, and checks who can be with him.
sharedPlan: GP calls 999 now and gives a clear handover; vascular team informed
Leg down, body warm with no direct heat on the leg, nil by mouth
After the emergency: DOAC discussion per NICE NG196, smoking and diabetes review
safetyNet: Re-call 999 if the leg becomes completely numb or he can’t move the foot, or chest pain or faintness
GP checks with the hospital the same day and arranges follow-up after discharge

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed in the first three minutes by accepting his label. The second trap is winning the argument and losing the patient: he must choose to go, and that means meeting the amputation fear.

items.fail: Accepting “my circulation’s worse” and sending painkillers or a diuretic.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious condition.” A sudden cold, pale, numb leg is acute limb ischaemia and only emergency vascular care helps.
items.fix: Ask when it started, whether it hurts at rest, and how it compares with the other foot. Sudden onset and numbness settle it.

items.fail: Booking a face-to-face appointment later today or an ABPI test.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Hours matter; any intermediate step wastes them.
items.fix: 999 ambulance and vascular handover now. Say who is calling and when.

items.why: Misses the likely cause and the secondary prevention that stops a repeat.
items.fix: “Your heart rhythm is probably where the clot came from” — then defer the anticoagulation talk until the leg is safe.

items.fail: Blaming him for declining the blood thinner.
items.why: “Does not respond appropriately to the patient’s emotions.” He becomes defensive and refuses.
items.fix: “The decision then isn’t the issue today; your leg is.”

items.fail: Overriding his refusal with authority instead of asking why.
items.why: The amputation fear is the hidden agenda; ignoring it loses the Relating marks and often the consent.
items.fix: “Is what happened to your friend behind not wanting to go in?” Then reframe: speed saves legs.

items.fail: Ending with “go to A&E” and no first aid or check of understanding.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no confirmed plan are standard failing statements.
items.fix: Leg down, warm body, nil by mouth, door open, re-call 999 if worse, then teach-back.
